bibliographic.title: Assessment of vaccine information accuracy across large language models
bibliographic.citation_apa: Siebielec, J., & Raciborski, F. (2026). Assessment of vaccine information accuracy across large language models. Frontiers in Public Health, 14, 1811462. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1811462

methodology.method_family: comparative LLM accuracy benchmarking with quantitative and qualitative answer analysis
methodology.study_design: cross-sectional comparison of four named LLMs answering 90 multiple-choice and two open-ended vaccination questions sourced from a government information website
methodology.sample_description: Four LLMs (ChatGPT, Copilot, DeepSeek, Gemini) queried with vaccination questions from a government information website; data collected March 2026
methodology.sample_size: 4 LLMs; 90 multiple-choice questions; 2 open-ended questions per model
methodology.technology_context: direct consumer LLM querying for vaccine and health information accuracy assessment

eligibility.exclusion_reason: The study empirically benchmarks factual accuracy of LLM responses to vaccination questions in a regulated health context but does not examine conversational governance, guardrails, observability, audit, compliance, human oversight, accountability, or operational control mechanisms.
eligibility.decision_rationale: Although the article is an empirical LLM study in healthcare and reports accuracy, safety-relevant usability limits, and government-sourced questions, the provided text contains no analysis of conversational systems governance, supervision workflows, monitoring infrastructure, auditability, or compliance frameworks central to the review scope.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Python triage marked borderline_manual (68/100) with moderate regulated-domain and LLM relevance but very low conversational and operational governance signals; adjudication should confirm exclusion despite contextual health-risk value.

appraisal.notes: Methods and results are clearly summarized in the abstract, but ethics, detailed protocols, and limitations are not evident in the provided excerpt.

cerqual.explanation: Findings on LLM vaccination-information accuracy are internally coherent within the excerpt, but the study does not address conversational governance mechanisms and therefore offers very low confidence for the review's core synthesis question.

coding.theme: LLM reliability as a health information source
coding.subtheme: vaccination information accuracy across consumer LLMs

synthesis.main_claim: Four tested LLMs performed well on multiple-choice vaccination questions, with Gemini highest (0.98) and ChatGPT lowest (0.86), but open-ended answers were factually correct yet too vague to be usable on their own as vaccine information sources.
synthesis.contribution: Provides comparative empirical evidence on accuracy and qualitative adequacy of LLM-generated vaccination information drawn from government website questions.
synthesis.limitations: Generated content was judged factually correct but lacking in detail; broader methodological and governance limitations are unclear from the provided text.
synthesis.use_in_review: Exclude from central or supporting governance evidence; at most peripheral contextual citation if the review separately documents ungoverned LLM health-information risk, not governance mechanisms.

evidence.claim: Study objective is to assess correctness of LLM-generated vaccine information.
evidence.excerpt: verifying the correctness of generated responses becomes extremely important

evidence.claim: Empirical comparison of four named LLMs using government-sourced vaccination questions.
evidence.excerpt: Four LLMs (ChatGPT, Copilot, DeepSeek, Gemini) were chosen for the analysis.

evidence.claim: Sample comprised 90 multiple-choice and two open-ended vaccination questions.
evidence.excerpt: All models were asked 90 multiple-choice questions on the various topics surrounding vaccination, sourced from a government information website.

evidence.claim: Models differed significantly in multiple-choice accuracy.
evidence.excerpt: Biggest proportion of correct answers was achieved by Gemini (0.98), smallest one – by ChatGPT (0.86).

evidence.claim: Open-ended answers were correct but insufficiently detailed for standalone use.
evidence.excerpt: the generated content, while factually correct, was not enough to be usable on its own.

evidence.claim: No conversational governance, oversight, audit, or compliance mechanisms are discussed in the provided text.
evidence.excerpt: Answers were analysed quantitatively and qualitatively.
Use of Large Language Models (LLMs) as a health information source is on the rise.
REVIEWED BY Oluchi Abosi, University of Iowa Health Care, United States
